facts: A two-storey terraced house built as a single dwelling; no units of living accommodation have been created in it since it was built. Its freehold owner, Mr Patel, a private individual who does not live there, manages it himself. He lets each of its five bedrooms to a different person under a separate tenancy, and each of them pays him a monthly rent. The occupants are Amy, Ben, Chloe, Dev and Ella, five friends; none is related to any other, and none is married to, in a civil partnership with, or living together as if married or as civil partners with any other. Each occupies the house as his or her residence for the purpose of undertaking a full-time course of higher education at a university. None occupies it as his or her only or main residence: each one's main residence is a parent's house. The five share the house's only kitchen (its only cooking facilities) and its only bathroom, which contains its only toilet and its only shower and basin. The accommodation has no use other than their occupation.

A three-bedroom semi-detached house built as a single dwelling; no units of living accommodation have been created in it since it was built. Its owner, Mrs Green, a private individual who does not live there, lets the whole house on one joint monthly tenancy to four people, who pay her the rent: Ben and his wife Anna, and Ben's brother Dan and Dan's wife Carol. Anna is not related by blood to Ben, Dan or Carol, and Carol is not related by blood to Ben, Dan or Anna. All four occupy the house as their only or main residence. They share its only kitchen and its only bathroom (with the only toilet, basin and bath). The accommodation has no use other than their occupation.

A four-bedroom detached house built as a single dwelling; no units of living accommodation have been created in it since it was built. A private landlord, Mr Owen, who does not live there, lets the whole house on one joint monthly tenancy to five people, who share the rent: Paul and Quinn, who are not married or civil partners but live together as if a married couple; Quinn's mother Rita; Paul's brother Simon; and Theo, the son of Paul's and Simon's sister (who lives elsewhere). Rita is not related by blood to Paul, Simon or Theo. All five occupy the house as their only or main residence. They share its only kitchen and its two bathrooms. The accommodation has no use other than their occupation.

A three-bedroom terraced house built as a single dwelling; no units of living accommodation have been created in it since it was built. A private landlord, Ms Shaw, who does not live there, lets it on a monthly tenancy to Lena, who pays her the rent. Lena lives there with three others: Max, her stepson (the son of Lena's late husband by his earlier marriage; Lena is not Max's mother); Olive, the daughter of Lena and her late husband, so that Max and Olive have the same father but different mothers; and Nora, Max's daughter. Lena is not married to, in a civil partnership with, or living as if married or as civil partners with anyone. All four occupy the house as their only or main residence. They share its only kitchen and its only bathroom. The accommodation has no use other than their occupation.

A four-bedroom house built as a single dwelling; no units of living accommodation have been created in it since it was built. A property company, Elm Lettings Ltd, which holds no registration as a provider of social housing or as a social landlord, lets it on a monthly tenancy to Xena and her husband Yusuf, who pay the rent. They live there with their daughter Zara; with Adam, who is placed with Xena and Yusuf as his foster parents under the Fostering Services Regulations 2002 and is not otherwise related to anyone in the house; and with Beth, whom Xena and Yusuf employ as a nanny to look after Zara and Adam. Looking after the children is the only work Beth does for anyone. Beth's room is supplied to her by Xena and Yusuf as part of the consideration for that work, and she pays no rent and gives nothing else for it. Beth is not related to anyone in the house. All five occupy the house as their only or main residence. They share its only kitchen and its only bathroom. The accommodation has no use other than their occupation.

A four-bedroom house built as a single dwelling; no units of living accommodation have been created in it since it was built. A private landlord, Mr Reid, who does not live there, lets it on a monthly tenancy to Craig and his wife Donna, who pay him the rent. They live there with their two sons, Eli and Finn, and with Gina, an au pair who looks after the boys; that is the only work Gina does for anyone. Donna supplies Gina's room to her as part of the consideration for that work, and Gina also pays Donna 40 pounds a week towards the room. Gina is not related to anyone in the house. All five occupy the house as their only or main residence. They share its only kitchen and its only bathroom. The accommodation has no use other than their occupation.

A large five-bedroom house built as a single dwelling; no units of living accommodation have been created in it since it was built. A private landlord, Lady Vane, who does not live there, lets it on a yearly tenancy to Sam and his wife Tina, who pay her the rent. Sam employs Pablo as a chauffeur, driving Sam and Tina on their private journeys; that is the only work Pablo does for anyone. Pablo lives in two rooms on the top floor of the house with his wife Rosa and their son Hugo; those rooms are supplied to Pablo by Sam as part of the consideration for his work, and neither Pablo, Rosa nor Hugo pays any rent or gives anything else for them. Rosa and Hugo do no work for Sam or Tina. Pablo, Rosa and Hugo are not related to Sam or Tina. All five occupy the house as their only or main residence. The top-floor rooms have no toilet, washing or cooking facilities of their own; all five share the house's only kitchen and its two bathrooms. The accommodation has no use other than their occupation.

A four-bedroom house built as a single dwelling; no units of living accommodation have been created in it since it was built. A private landlord, Mr Fox, who does not live there, lets it on a monthly tenancy to Victor, who pays him the rent. Victor is an adult placement carer approved under the Adult Placement Schemes (England) Regulations 2004, providing care in this house for three service users under a scheme permitted by those Regulations: Wendy, Yasmin and Zac, who live there with him. Each of the three pays Victor a weekly sum for accommodation and care. None of the four is related to, married to, in a civil partnership with, or living as if married or as civil partners with any other. All four occupy the house as their only or main residence. They share its only kitchen and its only bathroom. The accommodation has no use other than their occupation.

A five-bedroom terraced house built as a single dwelling; no units of living accommodation have been created in it since it was built. Its freehold owner, Mrs Hill, a private individual who does not live there and has no connection with the occupants' employer, lets each bedroom under a separate weekly agreement, and each occupant pays her a weekly rent. The occupants are Alan, Brian, Colin, Derek and Ed, unrelated men, each a British citizen employed all year round by a building contractor on a nearby site. Each stays in the house from Monday to Friday. None occupies it as his only or main residence: each one's main residence is his own house in another town. None is a student, none is an asylum seeker, and none has left his home because of violence or threats. They share the house's only kitchen and its only bathroom. The accommodation has no use other than their occupation.

A farmhouse built as a single dwelling; no units of living accommodation have been created in it since it was built. It is owned and managed by Orchard Farms Ltd, a fruit-growing company, which provides it to five of its employees: their occupation is made partly in consideration of their employment with the company in the United Kingdom, and each also pays the company a weekly charge for it, deducted from wages. Petra, Radu and Sanna each have leave to remain granted by virtue of residence scheme immigration rules and have taken up employment in the United Kingdom with Orchard Farms Ltd; none of them occupies the farmhouse as his or her only or main residence (each one's main residence is a home abroad). Tom and Ursula are British citizens employed by Orchard Farms Ltd to pick fruit, work whose nature depends on the cycle of the seasons and recurs automatically each year, and whose duration under their contracts cannot exceed eight months; neither occupies the farmhouse as his or her only or main residence (each one's main residence is a parent's house). None of the five is related to, married to, in a civil partnership with, or living as if married or as civil partners with any other. They share the farmhouse's only kitchen and its two bathrooms. The accommodation has no use other than their occupation.

A five-bedroom house built as a single dwelling; no units of living accommodation have been created in it since it was built. It is managed by Northgate Housing Ltd, a private company that holds no registration as a provider of social housing or as a social landlord. Its occupants are Ahmed and his daughter Bella, and Chidi, Dawit and Emil. Ahmed, Chidi, Dawit and Emil are each an asylum seeker (section 94 of the Immigration and Asylum Act 1999) provided with this accommodation under section 95 of that Act, funded by the National Asylum Support Service; Bella is a dependant of Ahmed provided with this accommodation in the same way. The National Asylum Support Service pays Northgate Housing Ltd for each occupant's accommodation. Apart from Ahmed and Bella, none of the five is related to any other, and none is married to, in a civil partnership with, or living as if married or as civil partners with any other. They share the house's only kitchen and its only bathroom. The accommodation has no use other than their occupation.

A large house built as a single dwelling; no units of living accommodation have been created in it since it was built. It is managed by Safe Harbour, a voluntary organisation and registered charity that holds no registration as a provider of social housing or as a social landlord. Safe Harbour uses the house wholly for the temporary accommodation of women, and their children, who have left their homes as a result of physical violence or threats of violence from men who are or were their husbands or with whom they were living. Its occupants are Carla and her two children, Kyle and Lily; Dina; and Erin, each woman having left her home for that reason. Apart from Carla and her children, none of the five is related to any other. Each woman pays Safe Harbour a weekly charge for the accommodation of herself and any children with her. They share the house's only kitchen and its two bathrooms. The accommodation has no use other than their occupation.

A two-bedroom terraced house built as a single dwelling; no units of living accommodation have been created in it since it was built. Its owner, Mr Lowe, a private individual who does not live there, lets it on a joint monthly periodic tenancy to Vera and Wanda, two friends who are not related and who are not married to, in a civil partnership with, or living as if married or as civil partners with each other. They pay him the rent and occupy the house as their only or main residence. They share its only kitchen and its only bathroom. The accommodation has no use other than their occupation.

A two-bedroom house built as a single dwelling; no units of living accommodation have been created in it since it was built. Fay holds the freehold of the house and occupies it as her only or main residence. She lets her spare bedroom to Gus, who pays her a weekly rent and occupies it as his only or main residence; Gus has no interest in the house other than that arrangement. Fay and Gus are not related and are not married to, in a civil partnership with, or living as if married or as civil partners with each other. They share the house's only kitchen and its only bathroom. The accommodation has no use other than their occupation.

A five-bedroom house built as a single dwelling; no units of living accommodation have been created in it since it was built. Hana and her husband Ivan hold the freehold jointly and occupy the house as their only or main residence. They let three of the bedrooms to Jack, Kim and Liam, each of whom pays them a weekly rent, has no interest in the house other than that arrangement, and occupies it as his or her only or main residence. Jack, Kim and Liam are not related to each other or to Hana or Ivan, and none of them is married to, in a civil partnership with, or living as if married or as civil partners with anyone in the house. All five share the house's only kitchen and its two bathrooms. The accommodation has no use other than their occupation.

A three-storey Victorian house, built as a single dwelling, in which units of living accommodation have been created since it was built: the ground floor is now Flat 1 and the first floor is now Flat 2, and the second floor is divided into three bedsitting rooms. Flat 1 lies wholly below the rest of the building and Flat 2 lies wholly above Flat 1. Each of the two flats is a separate set of rooms with its own front door and its own kitchen, toilet, basin and shower, used only by the people living in that flat. Each bedsitting room has a sink and a cooker for its occupant's use alone; the three bedsitting rooms share one bathroom on the second-floor landing, which contains the only toilet and shower available to their occupants. The freeholder, Mr Hart, a private individual who does not live in the building, lets each flat and each bedsitting room on a separate tenancy, and every tenant pays him rent. Flat 1 is occupied by Kemal and his wife Leah; Flat 2 by Leo; the bedsitting rooms by Mia, Nico and Omar, one each. Apart from Kemal and Leah, none of the six is related to, married to, in a civil partnership with, or living as if married or as civil partners with any other. All six occupy their accommodation as their only or main residence. The accommodation has no use other than their occupation.

A four-storey building, built as a single dwelling and later converted into four flats, one on each floor, each lying wholly above or below the others; each flat has its own front door and its own kitchen, toilet, basin and shower, used only by the people living in it. The building contains no other living accommodation. The building is a converted block of flats to which section 257 applies. No HMO declaration under section 255 is in force in respect of it. The freehold is held by a religious order, which manages the building; none of the occupants has any interest in it beyond a licence from the order. The building is occupied principally for the purposes of a religious community whose principal occupation is prayer and contemplation. Each flat is occupied by two members of the community, eight people in all (Aaron and Basil; Cyril and Dominic; Edmund and Felix; Gareth and Hugh), none of whom is related to, married to, in a civil partnership with, or living as if married or as civil partners with any other. Each member pays the order a monthly contribution for his board and lodging and occupies his flat as his only or main residence. The accommodation has no use other than their occupation.

A single-storey bungalow, built as one house, in which units of living accommodation have been created since it was built: building works divided it into five studios opening off a common hallway. No part of the building lies above or below any other part. Each studio has its own kitchen area with a cooker and its own shower room with a toilet, basin and shower, used only by its occupant; nothing else in the building contains a toilet, washing facilities or cooking facilities, and the hallway is the only shared space. The owner, Mrs Kaur, a private individual who does not live there, lets each studio on a separate tenancy and each tenant pays her rent. The occupants are Pia, Rhys, Saul, Tess and Umar, one to a studio; none is related to, married to, in a civil partnership with, or living as if married or as civil partners with any other. Each occupies the studio as his or her only or main residence. The accommodation has no use other than their occupation.

A three-storey building constructed as a shop on the ground floor with two flats above it, Flat 1 on the first floor and Flat 2 on the second floor; it has not been altered and no units of living accommodation have been created in it since it was built. Flat 2 lies wholly above Flat 1 and the shop. Flat 2 has its own front door at the top of the common stairs, its own kitchen, and its own bathroom with a toilet, basin and shower, all used only by the people living in Flat 2. The freeholder, Mr Burns, a private individual who does not live in the building, lets Flat 2 to five people on separate tenancies of a room each, and each pays him rent: Ava, Bram, Cleo, Dara and Evan, none of whom is related to, married to, in a civil partnership with, or living as if married or as civil partners with any other. All five occupy Flat 2 as their only or main residence and share its kitchen and bathroom. Flat 2 has no use other than their occupation.

A six-storey block constructed as six flats, one on each floor, and not altered since; no units of living accommodation have been created in it since it was built, and it contains no other living accommodation. Each flat has its own front door off the common stairs, its own kitchen, and its own bathroom with a toilet, basin and bath, used only by the people living in that flat. Flat 4, on the fourth floor, lies wholly above Flats 1 to 3 and wholly below Flats 5 and 6. Its long leaseholder, Mr Dyer, who does not live in the block, lets Flat 4 to five people on separate tenancies of a room each, and each pays him rent: Faye, Gil, Hugo, Iris and Joel, none of whom is related to, married to, in a civil partnership with, or living as if married or as civil partners with any other. All five occupy Flat 4 as their only or main residence and share its kitchen and bathroom. Flat 4 has no use other than their occupation.

A six-bedroom house built as a single dwelling; no units of living accommodation have been created in it since it was built. It is owned and managed by Westshire NHS Trust; the manager is a health service body within section 9 of the National Health Service Act 2006. The trust lets each bedroom on a separate licence to one of six nurses it employs: Kate, Lara, Mona, Nell, Ola and Pam, none of whom is related to, married to, in a civil partnership with, or living as if married or as civil partners with any other. Each pays the trust a monthly rent and occupies the house as her only or main residence. They share its only kitchen and its two bathrooms. The accommodation has no use other than their occupation.

A five-bedroom house built as a single dwelling; no units of living accommodation have been created in it since it was built. The building is social housing within the meaning of Part 2 of the Housing and Regeneration Act 2008, and the manager is a profit-making registered provider of social housing, Brightway Homes Ltd, which is not registered as a social landlord under Part 1 of the Housing Act 1996. Brightway lets each bedroom on a separate tenancy to one of five tenants who each pay it rent: Quentin, Rosa, Stan, Tara and Uri, none of whom is related to, married to, in a civil partnership with, or living as if married or as civil partners with any other. Each occupies the house as his or her only or main residence. They share its only kitchen and its two bathrooms. The accommodation has no use other than their occupation.

A six-bedroom house built as a single dwelling; no units of living accommodation have been created in it since it was built. It is owned and managed by Greenway Housing Co-operative Ltd, which is registered as a co-operative society under the Co-operative and Community Benefit Societies Act 2014, is not a registered provider of social housing of any kind, and is not registered as a social landlord under Part 1 of the Housing Act 1996. The society's rules secure that: membership is restricted to persons who are occupiers or prospective occupiers of buildings it manages or controls; all its management decisions are made by the members at a general meeting which all members are entitled to, and invited to, attend; each member has equal voting rights at such a meeting; and anyone who occupies premises in its buildings without being a member does so only as a result of sharing occupation with a member at the member's invitation. The occupants are five members, Vic, Will, Xia, Yves and Zoe, and Zoe's partner Amir, who is not a member and lives there at Zoe's invitation, sharing her room; Zoe and Amir live together as if a married couple. No one else in the house is related to, married to, in a civil partnership with, or living as if married or as civil partners with any other. Each member occupies a room under a licence from the society and pays it a weekly charge; nobody who occupies the house holds a tenancy of any kind, so none holds an assured, secure or protected tenancy. All six occupy the house as their only or main residence and share its only kitchen and its two bathrooms. The accommodation has no use other than their occupation.

A large house built as a single dwelling; no units of living accommodation have been created in it since it was built. The freehold is held by a religious order, which manages the house; none of the occupants has any interest in it beyond a licence from the order. The building is occupied principally for the purposes of a religious community whose principal occupation is prayer and contemplation. Its occupants are six members of the community, Agnes, Bridget, Cecily, Dorothy, Edith and Frances, none of whom is related to, married to, in a civil partnership with, or living as if married or as civil partners with any other. Each pays the order a monthly contribution for her board and lodging and occupies the house as her only or main residence. They share its only kitchen and its two bathrooms. The accommodation has no use other than their occupation. The building is not a converted block of flats to which section 257 applies, and no HMO declaration under section 255 is in force in respect of it.

Riverside House is a four-storey building, built as a single dwelling and later converted into four flats, one on each floor; it is a converted block of flats to which section 257 applies. Flat 3, on the second floor, lies wholly above Flats 1 and 2 and wholly below Flat 4; it has its own front door, its own kitchen, and its own bathroom with a toilet, basin and shower, used only by the people living in Flat 3. Ivy holds a lease of Flat 3 granted for a term of 125 years and occupies it as her only or main residence. She lets two of its bedrooms to Jon and Kara, each of whom pays her a weekly rent, has no interest in the flat other than that arrangement, and occupies it as his or her only or main residence. Ivy, Jon and Kara are not related to, married to, in a civil partnership with, or living as if married or as civil partners with each other. The three share Flat 3's kitchen and bathroom. Flat 3 has no use other than their occupation. No HMO declaration under section 255 is in force in respect of Flat 3.

A five-bedroom house built as a single dwelling; no units of living accommodation have been created in it since it was built. Its owner, Mrs Moss, a private individual who does not live there, lets each bedroom on a separate tenancy to one of five tenants who each pay her rent: Bea, Cal, Dot, Ezra and Flo, none of whom is related to, married to, in a civil partnership with, or living as if married or as civil partners with any other. Each occupies the house as his or her only or main residence. They share its only kitchen, its only bathroom and its ground-floor living room. Their occupation is not the only use of the accommodation: on weekdays Mrs Moss runs a hairdressing business, open to the public, in that living room. An HMO declaration under section 255 is in force in respect of the building. The building is not a converted block of flats to which section 257 applies.

A purpose-built block of forty study bedrooms in England, owned and managed by a university, occupied solely by students undertaking full-time courses of higher education at that university, who share kitchens and bathrooms in groups of eight and pay the university rent. The facts do not say whether any regulations under Schedule 14 paragraph 3A specify the university or a description of establishment or manager that includes it.

A five-bedroom house in Cardiff, Wales, built as a single dwelling, let by a private landlord on separate tenancies to five unrelated adults who each pay rent, occupy it as their only or main residence, and share its kitchen and bathroom.

A five-bedroom house built as a single dwelling, let by a private landlord on separate tenancies to five unrelated adults who each pay rent, occupy it as their only or main residence, and share its kitchen and bathroom. The question asked is whether the landlord must hold a licence for it under Part 2 and whether a licence is currently in force.

A five-bedroom house let to five unrelated tenants who share its kitchen and bathroom, whose living room is also used by the landlord as a shop on weekdays. No HMO declaration is in force. The question asked is whether the local housing authority ought to make an HMO declaration under section 255 in respect of it.

A house converted into three flats, one on each floor, each with its own kitchen and bathroom used only by its occupants; the conversion works did not comply with building regulations at the time. Two of the flats are let to tenants and one is occupied by its long leaseholder. The facts do not state whether the building is a converted block of flats to which section 257 applies, and no HMO declaration is in force.

A six-bedroom house managed by a society registered as a co-operative society under the Co-operative and Community Benefit Societies Act 2014, not a registered provider of social housing nor a registered social landlord, whose rules secure all the conditions in Schedule 14 paragraph 2B(2). Six unrelated members each occupy a room under a weekly periodic tenancy granted by the society, pay rent, occupy the house as their only or main residence and share its kitchen and bathrooms. The facts do not state whether any of the tenancies is an assured, secure or protected tenancy.

A five-bedroom house built as a single dwelling, let by a private landlord on separate tenancies to five unrelated adults who each pay rent, occupy it as their only or main residence, and share its kitchen and bathroom. The managing agent is a local housing authority. The question is asked for the purposes of Part 1 of the Housing Act 2004 (housing conditions).

A house in which eight unrelated adults live, each paying a weekly fee, sharing its kitchen and bathrooms; the house is run as a residential care establishment whose occupation is regulated under another enactment. The facts do not say which enactment, and the file does not contain the Schedule of enactments referred to in regulation 6(1) of SI 2006/373.
